I wish to say one final word about controls. We are getting rid of controls as rapidly as we can. Controls based on scarcity are pretty well gone. But controls that have to do with the cost of living are being and must be retained if we wish to protect the economy that we have built up during the war years, and I think it is an economy to be proud of. For example, if we took the control off lumber, which seems to be an irksome control, there would either be no lumber in Canada, or users in Canada would pay anywhere up to $20 a thousand more for their lumber. Without the control, the lumber would move across the line, where prices are vastly higher. That is why we keep the control on lumber. There are reasons, and sound reasons, I believe, for every control that is being maintained at this time.
Let me say this. The controllers who are being criticized in this house from time to time have, during an acute period of shortage, seen that Canadian citizens were supplied with their requirements. We have had, for instance, to restrict the use of gasoline. Nevertheless, the controllers have seen that when a coupon was issued for gasoline, the gasoline was there in the pump to honour the coupon, and Canada is the only country I know of in the world that has been able to keep that position.
Therefore, I say, let us not be too critical of the work of these controllers. Theirs has been a difficult task. It has been difficult to keep them at their task for the time sufficient to remove the controls in an orderly way. Scarcity controls are going rapidly or have already gone. As time goes on, history, I think, will treat kindly the work of the controllers in Canada's war period.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset may I, on behalf of the members of this group, express
The Address-Mr. Gillis

our very deep regret at the news we received this afternoon of the passing of the late Norman McLarty. Some of us in this group had the privilege of sitting in this house with him for five years, and we got to know him and to like him. He was always a very courteous gentleman, regardless of our differences in politics, and through you we should like to express to his family our deepest sympathy.
In rising to take part in this debate, I am reminded very much of the parliament of 1940. In that parliament, meeting for the first time when we were engaged in one of the greatest conflicts the world has ever seen, the problem that faced the government and the members of the house was the changing over of our economy from peace to war. It was a difficult task; it took a long time, and many mis< takes were made. Nevertheless, perhaps despite the government, this country made a substantial contribution to the winning of that conflict.
This also is a new parliament. We have here approximately ninety new members. The war is over. It is the responsibility now of this new parliament, and of the same government, to transform our economy from war to peace. That also will be a difficult task, one that will require the patience and understanding of everyone in this house. But we cannot afford to make mistakes at this stage of the game, because we cannot afford to quibble over the future of those who fought the war on the field of battle and are now returning to us. Nor dare we quibble over those employed in industry who provided the sinews of war which were vital to our fighting troops.
During the process of fighting the war this country had a national objective around which we could rally our people. That objective was the winning of the war, the defeating of totalitarianism abroad, and preserving on this continent that framework of democracy within which we have sufficient freedom to go forward into a better future. But at the present time, as far as I can see, we have no national objective. That national objective must be established. The people of this country must be given leadership and rallied around certain objectives for which they think they fought this war.
Our leader, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), set out briefly, in seven or eight points, the things which we think the government should be doing at this time in order to give the necessary leadership to the country. His points were plain and very simple.
First, we believe that the people of this country waged this war in order to improve

their standard of living-the standard of living of all Canadians-and it can stand considerable improvement, even the standard established during this war.
Second, we believe that everyone in this country is entitled to a decent home to live in, at a reasonable cost.
Third, we believe that the federal government must accept greater financial responsibility in the field of education and that the educational standards across Canada must be raised in some parts and made uniform throughout the dominion. We believe that the teaching profession must be given greater recognition in the job they have to do in building the future citizens of Canada.
Fourth, we believe that all the people of this country are entitled to something in the way of social security. We believe that this government should as soon as possible bring down a national social security act, to be administered under one department, which will remove the fear of insecurity from the minds of our people, a fear that they have had over a long period of time. We believe that our aged people should be cared for and that the youth of the country are entitled to better standard than they have had in the past.
These, Mr. Speaker, are the objectives for which we think we have fought this war. But in listening to the discussions in this house and in travelling across this country it seems to me that there are two opposing groups in Canada who fought this war for two entirely different reasons.
The working people of Canada, and that includes the farmers, the fishermen, the industrial workers and the small business people, fought this war to preserve this framework of democracy within which they could establish within this country, when the war was over, the things that we visualized we were fighting this war for; that is, to eliminate the conditions that breed war. On the other hand, watching the struggle to-day, we find that the owning classes in this country, those who control the means of life, claim our resources and are administering all of our economic processes. I am led to believe, by some discussions I have heard in the house, that the reason they fought this war is to preserve the status quo and to get back to 1939 as soon as possible. That is the impression I got from the discussion. You hear men say, "We still believe in the system of private enterprise." The government accepts that slogan; the Conservative party to my right accept it; the fact of the matter is that every

The Address-Mr. Gillis
part of this house other than the members of the group for whom I am speaking to-night accepts it.
What is this so-called free enterprise or private enterprise? I want someone at some time in this chamber to rise in his place and define it. What are the plans of free enterprise for the future? We must not forget that under that system of free enterprise we have had three wars in one lifetime-the Boer war, the great war, and now this last conflict. If the system of free enterprise can bring about for us the social objectives for which we fought this war, we should not have had the last two wars. They have had three opportunities in the past over a lifetime to prove that they can do these things, and they have not succeeded. Personally I think conditions in the world to-day with the prospect of wars in the future are such that we cannot afford to take the chance of any more wars, because if we do, it will perhaps mean the end of civilization.
I was interested in listening last Thursday evening to the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. Macdonnell). He made an excellent speech. However, I was struck by a few of the phrases he used. For example, he built up a nice story in favour of the maintenance of what he calls private enterprise, and I sat here thinking I would like to get his definition- of it. I hope that some time before the house rises he will tell us exactly where there exists in this country to-day private enterprise as we have had it in the past. There is no such thing. For example, he stated that the system of private enterprise should be maintained, that those who are risking their capital are entitled to a profit on it. Well, there is no one risking an-y capital in this country to-day, and they have not been risking any capital all during the process of fighting this war.
I happened to sit on the reconstruction committee for some three years, and during that period we had the privilege of examining practically every business organization in this country which would be giving employment in the post-war period. They came in and gave us their plans; they told us what they were prepared to do, but they all wound up with the same statement: they were prepared to do that, contingent upon the federal government making available the capital necessary and guaranteeing the profits. So, you see, none of these people were prepared to risk any capital.
The situation, as I see it to-day, thinking the thing over quickly, is this. The government has established the industrial development bank. Any risk entering into the establishment of new industry after the war will be underwritten by the government through that bank. It is going to underwrite the profits. In the field of housing the federal government has handed over to the major insurance companies the building of houses, and is underwriting the risk. In fact there is no risk. In mining the same thing applies. The federal government is expected to carry on the geological surveys and to send out the prospectors. If a prospector makes a discovery he reports it to some mining company. The mining company then carries on the development and makes the money. In lumbering the same thing is true: the government will build the base roads into the timber; they will improve the waterways for driving purposes; the *workmen will go in and cut down the lumber for very inadequate wages; but all the initial outlay in developing the timber resources, fire prevention, and so on-for all those things the government pays the shot; someone else steps in and makes the money.
The whole picture across Canada to-day is as I have described it. If the government is expected to carry on and develop the resources, take the risk, and make this investment, why should the government not take the profits, and turn them back ultimately to the working people of this country on the basis of social security, to give them some reward, when they are through with their labours, other than the scrap heap which they have had from generation to generation?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: "Depreciation."

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Oh, no, they have no depreciation; they just "get the axe," and stagger away to an old man's home, if they can find one. In most of the provinces there is not any place that will accept them.
So, thinking in terms of seventy-five years ago, I can understand the philosophy of the Liberal party, the Conservative party and the Social Credit party in the maintenance of free enterprise. But it no longer exists. What we have to-day straight across this country is four or five large monopolies in every field, which have set up holding companies, driven out the small shareholders, and concentrated power completely in the hands of a very few individuals who to-day wield economic dictatorship over the whole country and largely dictate the policy of any government which is in power which tries to play ball with them and maintain things as they were in 1939.
Getting back to 1939, I heard an hon. member across the way say that they did not want a new social order, that things were all right as they were, remove the controls and get back to where we were. What did we fight
The Address-Mr. Gillis

this war for? To go back there? Those who fought this war with certain objectives in mind had no such intentions, and anyone who takes that attitude today is completely out of touch with the world picture. You cannot get back there if you want to. We can struggle and continue to use on that basis this House of Commons or the legislatures we still have across this country, and we can do what they did in Europe-bring our house of cards down around our ears. To-day we have to recognize the fact that certain economic reforms must be made in this country; otherwise it is not possible for us to enjoy freedom, democracy, and the things for which our service personnel fought this war.
The hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario-I am not trying to pick on him particularly, but certain phrases he used jarred on me-also had this to say: you have a right to exploit your fellow-man and take a profit for it, because of the risk. He said that every worker who demands a wage increase is demanding a profit. That is not my conception of profits. Then, of course, he said that the worker was not taking any risk. I should like to ask him if he ever checked the industrial casualty lists of Canada. Those who go to the sea in boats, those who are employed in the mining industry, the steel plants, and so forth, across this country; check the figures year by year and you will find that their casualties greatly outnumber those of war. See them creeping around suffering from silicosis, going prematurely to their graves, without reward of any kind. I should like to have the hon. member on the east coast and put him in a boat with the shore fishers at four o'clock in the morning, to go out and set his traps and pull his trawls. He puts perhaps $1,500 worth of gear into the water this morning; to-morrow a storm comes up and the whole thing is gone. He is wiped out and it will take ten years for him to get that gear together again. There is plenty of risk there. Or go into the coal mines of Nova Scotia with a coal miner, at five o'clock in the morning. That man goes some six miles under the Atlantic ocean, working eight hours with nothing on but a pair of shoes and overalls. There are many casualties in that industry, and after a man has drawn his meagre pittance and budgeted on a deficit every week for years for himself and his family, if he lives to be seventy he will be given a cane and'asked to make his way to the nearest poorhouse. There is no depreciation, no reward, no consideration. The risk which the industrial worker takes is physical. My hon. friend was thinking in terms of money, but we have to get away from that philosophy. In the future this country has to
rMr. Gillis.]
think in terms of human life and the needs and rights of human beings; otherwise we have fought another war for nothing.
Take the business man who is managing his own business. He draws a certain amount per week and what he takes out for managing his business is a wage for services rendered. What I would consider a profit for the average worker across the country would be this: provided that he had a job which would pay sufficient wages for him to meet all obligations, rent, fuel, family requirements, and with a sufficient income to send his children to university, if he could bank a thousand a year, that would be profit, but there is no industrial worker and there are few farmers with that kind of set-up.
I am not trying to lecture my hon. friends, but I make this statement because I am convinced that, after private enterprise has been given a chance to fight three wars, throwing men into war, giving them a uniform and then taking it off them and putting them on the street, and then telling them to get ready for the next war, that day is gone, and we shall not have that chance again. We must therefore change our philosophy in this house. It is the job of every member in this house representing a constituency in Canada to study the subject himself, not on the basis of slogans or on the basis of things as they were in the past. The job that has to be done now in Canada is to live up to the promises made our service personnel and our industrial workers during the process of fighting the war.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) spoke of a new world, a new philosophy, something new that was to come out of this war. But it seems to me that we have the same old order, the same old philosophy, because the basic thing that some people apparently are thinking about is money and getting back to where we were in 1939.
I wish to say a few words now to the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Mackenzie), who I regret is not in his place at the moment. He has a large department and there will have to be a good deal of discussion in the house before this session closes. There is one matter I consider of urgent importance that comes within his jurisdiction. The speech from the throne intimates that there is to be established a veterans' charter. That is all right, but I am getting a little tired of slogans, and unless that charter means something I am not very much concerned about it. Centering veterans' problems in one department with sympathetic administration is a good thing and if that is what the charter means I am all for it. But I wish to call attention to this particularly. Coming back to this country

The Address-Mr. Gillis
to-day from overseas is a large number of service personnel, boys who committed some misdemeanour, some slight infraction of military law and who were sentenced to detention on the other side, many of them to two or three years. I have seen copies of some courts martial; I have seen where a boy was sentenced to three years on the other side after having two and a half years of combat service, and some of these boys have been sentenced after the close of the war in Germany. A large number of these boys are being brought back to the country. They are taken first to Kingston and then sent back to then-respective district depots and are discharged and sent to some civilian prison in Canada to complete sentence.
I have written to the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) and have been in touch for some time with the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Abbott). I claim that for an infraction of military law they cannot send a boy after discharge to a civilian prison in order to complete his sentence. I have not had any definite word from either of the ministers as to whether I am right or wrong on that point, from the legal point of view, and I do not care particularly whether I am, because what I am thinking about is this. I know of one case where a boy had two and a half years of combat service. He went through Italy, and into Germany till the war was over. He picked up a couple of army blankets one night and went and sold them to get some wine-many hon. members will understand that. That boy was sentenced to three years. He has a wife and two children. A civilian picked up on that charge in Canada would get a fine or a month or two in one of the county gaols. What has that boy got? He was sentenced to three years, fined all his gratuity, and in addition to that he is placed in a civilian prison so that he will come out with the stigma of a convict. His wife and children lose their allowance. He is dishonourably discharged and that will militate against him for the rest of his natural life. No recognition-whatsoever is given for services during the period of fighting the war.
What this house should press for is the setting up immediately of a parliamentary committee on veterans affairs where all these matters can be analysed by members. I believe there are seventy members in this house who are veterans either of the last war or of this one, and they should be given an opportunity as soon as possible to get together and look over the veterans' charter, examining all legislation, because it requires examination. No legislation is effective or worth the paper it is written on unless it is administered 47696-16
properly. I am not going to take more time on this subject, because I know that later on it will receive a good deal of discussion. The whole matter of rehabilitation calls for considerable checking up.
I would say a word or two to the minister of munitions, who has just spoken. I would judge from the talk he gave that he is Canada's greatest optimist, to say the least. The picture he painted in 'the field of employment across Canada is certainly not true in the province from which I come.

speechtext: He has to be an optimist to tackle the problem.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: But optimism, speeches and statistics will not solve that problem. Jobs have to be found and wages must be paid.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: You cannot solve the problem by a negative approach.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
It is not a matter of being negative or positive; it is a matter of finding out what you can do and getting busy and going after it. The unemployment problem is pretty bad in Nova Scotia. In January, 1944, the reconstruction committee tabled in this house a report that meant something from the point of view of employment as far as Nova Scotia is concerned. They decided then to build a causeway across the strait of Canso and to double-track the mainland from Sydney to Moncton, tearing up the old one and taking out the grades and curves. That would give considerable employment to the people of Nova Scotia at the present time. It would perhaps take up the slack while you are getting ready to find out what you intend to do in the next year or so. When the minister gets an opportunity I should like him to tell the house exactly what progress has been made with respect to bridging the strait of Canso and so forth, because that is one of the province's major post-war projects. I see it as a cushion in the reconversion period which could take care of a lot of the people coming out of the services and out of the war industries. There is no reconversion in Nova Scotia; it is a matter of closing out the industries and putting the workers back on the street. The project to which I have referred means something down there, and I should like to know what progress is being made.
Then I should like to get a statement from the Department of Reconstruction with respect to the coal commission. The coal mining industry of Canada is a very sick one. It requires considerable reorganization. The government recognized that, because it appointed a royal commission that is inquiring into the coal industry all across Canada

The Address-Mr. Gillis

with the view of reorganizing the industry and establishing a fuel policy. That commission has been on the road for some considerable time. I would urge the minister to render it every assistance and to do everything possible within his department to have the report of that commission brought down as early as possible. I believe they are completing their hearings in Sydney at the present time: It should not take very long to analyse those hearings and bring in a report. That industry certainly requires reorganization. Coupled with that is the whole steel set-up in the province. I am not going to go into that now. I noted that the minister tabled an order in council in the house on September 7 dealing with subsidies for the Dominion Steel and Coal industry. The number of that order is 1952. That order is very generous. Perhaps that generosity is required, but it certainly indicates that there is something wrong with that industry. The subsidy paid during 1943 was some 89,678,829.49. Well, an industry that has to get money poured into it like that should have some public supervision; it certainly is not private enterprise. Under private enterprise that assistance is necessary, and I am glad to see that according to this order in council the assistance is to be continued. The agreement has been extended into 1945.

CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset of the few remarks I desire to make I wish to add my congratulations to the mover and the seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. It is noteworthy that each hon. gentleman represents a distinguished branch of the service, the air force and the navy; and I might add with some pride that the mover of the address, the youthful member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Benidick-son) happens to be my house office mate. Even if he is from the bush country, to which the Minister of Reconstruction (Mr. Howe) referred, he is a good scout, and I think he will get along. In order that there may be no confusion as to the riding I represent, I should like to make it clear, particularly to new members, that there are two Waterloo ridings, Waterloo North and Waterloo South. Some misunderstanding seems to exist in the house and in some press reports with regard to the members representing these two constituencies. It has been said that "east is east and west is west and never the twain shall meet." The same might be said of the
The Address-Mr. Breithaupt

two Waterloos; north is north and south is south, and never the twain shall meet. This applies only, however, to the political philosophy of the two representatives, and has nothing to do with their personal relationships. As far as the two ridings are concerned, our interests are mutual to a large extent. They are both highly agricultural and highly industrial, and many Canadian insurance companies have their headquarters there. The town of Waterloo, which is in my riding, is often said to be the Hartford of Canada.
So much for my little sales talk on behalf of my riding, which I think every hon. member is quite justified in making. I join with other hon. members of this house in giving thanks to Almighty God for the success of allied arms and the complete and unconditional surrender of our axis enemies. I am particularly pleased at the presence in this house of one who so recently languished in a German prison camp where he had been confined, together with a very near relative of mine, Lieutenant Arthur Breithaupt of the Calgary Tanks, ever since the memorable storming of the beaches of Dieppe by Canadian armed forces. I refer, of course, to the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Merritt). In my maiden speech in this house after Dieppe, I recommended to the government that Cecil Merritt be made a senator upon his return to Canada, in recognition of his outstanding services. Hon. members who were here at that time will recall that suggestion. Apparently this was not to be, and he decided to enter parliament the hard way. In spite of the fact that he sits on the opposition benches, I wish to pay him a well earned tribute, quite apart from his political affiliations. His maiden speech delivered the other day has been the subject of much favourable comment even by many Liberal members, some of whom have said that the Liberal thought expressed therein would almost entitle the hon. gentleman to cross the floor of the house to the government benches. His criticisms were both fair and constructive, so we might still make him a senator.
At this time I wish to pay a very respectful and heartfelt tribute on behalf of my constituents as well as myself to those members of Canada's armed forces from Waterloo North and the entire Dominion of Canada who laid down their lives for a just and great cause, to free the world from tyranny and oppression. May we prove ourselves worthy of their great sacrifice.
During the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne I have heard from opposition parties a good deal of critical 
and sometimes unfair comment in regard to the government. I agree with the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) that we all make mistakes. I make plenty of them; so do the opposition parties, and even the government sometimes makes a few. My conception of the duty of a supporter of the government is that he should not only commend the government for good work done but also suggest where improvements can be effected. The trust placed by the Canadian people in such generous measure in our great leader, the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and his historic party in 1940, when he received a record majority, was certainly not misplaced. The clear mandate at that time was to win the war. The Prime Minister and his party have kept Canada united in spite of some talk we hear from opposition parties; they have delivered the goods, and the war has been won. To my mind actions speak louder than words. If in the post-war period every Canadian citizen assumes his share of the burden and pulls a strong oar, surely even the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. Macdonnell), who made such a strong plea for leadership and guidance, will have to admit that this country really has had it. It has had that leadership for many years past, and again the people of Canada saw fit to entrust the fortunes of this great country to the Liberal party. I would point out that recently another record has been set up to the credit of the Prime Minister; that is, that after having led the country to victory his government was returned to office. So far as I know never before in Canadian history has a government been returned after a period of war administration.
A good deal has been said on the subjects of reconstruction, reconversion and housing. I am a realist, and my training is to face facts and deal with them accordingly. I am firmly of the opinion that we cannot change over from a war-time economy to a peace-time economy as speedily as some people think we can. There is bound to be more or less dislocation. At the ending of a war we cannot 'be expected to continue to manufacture munitions and war equipment merely to employ labour. Even at that I firmly beileve that at the present time there is no actual shortage of jobs in Canada. The figures given by the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Howe) this evening further verifies that fact. In fact I know there are many communities, including the industrial centres in Waterloo North, which are actually experiencing a far greater shortage of help and far more absenteeism at the present time than they did at any time during the war. While it is true that there is

The Address-Mr. Breithaupt
not an over-all shortage of jobs in Canada, nevertheless it is true that there is a shortage of jobs in some localities where war plants previously existed. Many of those who migrated to some cities to work in temporary munitions and manufacturing centres should, in my humble opinion, bring themselves to the point where they see the wisdom of returning to their former abodes throughout the length and breadth of this country.
Much concern has been shown over the fact that there is a shortage of housing accommodation in many communities where war-time production reached an all-time high. Right here I wish to sound a note of caution. It seems to me that necessary as additional housing may be in some communities, such as those communities which are expanding their peacetime production or such communities as the cities and towns in my riding where diversified industry is characteristic of the locality, there is grave danger that in other districts an over-extended housing programme may backfire when adjustment and filtering back home of much of the urban populace take place.
While I am on the subject of housing, I should like to refer to the fact that the government plans to have insurance companies and limited dividend corporations build houses on a large scale. These plans are commendable. However, the fact should not be lost sight of that throughout the country there are many small builders who have started from scratch, who could, if given a greater chance, contribute greatly to the alleviation of the present housing situation. The figures given by the Minister of Reconstruction in this connection are impressive, that 38,000 homes have been built by smaller builders. This is only a start and many small builders would be pleased to amplify this programme, as well as other individuals who are capable and willing to build their own homes, if the granting of permits and the loosening up of building materials were simplified.
Personally I think the Department of Reconstruction is doing a good job under an able minister, but I respectfully submit that a good deal of the red tape and delay in the issuing of permits by the construction controller's department should be removed. We are sympathetic with the department in the enormous amount of work that they have to do, but I think a little word from the minister in this connection would be quite in order.
May I suggest also to the minister that the green light might now be given to a much greater extent in the issuing of permits for plant extensions and additions where such will assist in the government's plans for the
creation of jobs. Surely it is a good policy to further encourage the expansion of industry for the manufacture of the much needed civilian products now in such short supply and thus provide jobs for returning personnel of the armed forces and for others who have faithfully discharged their duties at home through the very difficult war years. Building materials such as cement and steel used in plant construction are not in any case in a critical position and are not generally used in volume for home construction.
I come now to the subject of meat rationing. As I said before, we all make mistakes. In my humble opinion it would appear that we as a government have definitely made one by putting into force a clumsy and complicated form of meat rationing at the end of a great world war. This comes at a time when reliable sources indicate that the United States is discontinuing meat rationing. Only a few months ago their supply position was more critical than ours. Merely because plans were made in Canada for meat rationing prior to the end of the Pacific war is in itself no reason why we should now proceed with it. No doubt some money has been spent on the preparation of this plan, but there is no reason to send good money after bad or to attempt to cover up an old mistake with a new one.
More meat products are apparently needed throughout the world than ever before, particularly in the United Kingdom. God knows Great Britain has stood by us through thick and thin during the most fateful hours of the war. We in turn owe her a great debt and should continue to stand by her in peace as we have done in war. In order that we may do this I have a suggestion to make. The cattle population of Canada is apparently in excess of all requirements, domestic and export. Let me therefore suggest that the government immediately put forward a plan to have meat production substantially increased so that these cattle may be processed. To do this, meat producers throughout the country, large and small, could, I am told, increase their production if further additional help is directed into the industry. If this does not entirely remedy the situation and floor space is the problem, I would suggest that the government lease some of its now idle munitions plants which the Minister of Reconstruction has told us to-night are not suitable for other purposes, to meat processors until such time as the situation has, by intelligent planning, been corrected. Let us get on with the job, but let us not saddle the country at this time with meat rationing.
The Address-Mr. Breithaupt

I wish to say a word about the proposal to have a national flag for Canada. I am all for the idea as long as the union jack forms an integral part of that flag.
The ministers of national defence for the various forces are to be complimented upon the efficient manner in which the return of the forces from overseas has been effected, and I wish to express the hope that a further speedup will result. I trust that the recent announcement which came through from London that there might be a shortage of ships because of certain movements in the Atlantic will not materialize and that everything will work out all right.
I understand that some of the army personnel are being kept in the armies of occupation against their wishes. Surely at this stage of the war service men and officers who have fought through bloody battles in Europe should be able to choose their own location and return home if they so desire. Since much confusion still exists in connection with releases and discharges from the armed services, I would suggest to the ministers that the latest regulations be sent forward to all members of parliament so that they can at least inform their constituencies intelligently as to up-to-date procedures.
Along with most Canadians I heartily approve the government's plan, as mentioned in the speech from the throne, to revise and clarify the definition of Canadian citizenship. This should have been accomplished many years ago.
I now come to what I consider to be the most important item in my speech. While prebudget comments on the subject of tax reduction made by our able Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley), and all the rest of the Liberal candidates, both on the hustings and in the house, lend some cause for hope, nevertheless I observe that in our present Canadian economy our people feel that a substantial tax reduction for all sections of the community is a positive commitment of the government.
During the stress and strain experienced during the war years people have been willing to take it on the chin and to bear the brunt of taxation so long as the patriotic urge of a final and complete victory over our enemies was in the process of being achieved. But now that the war is over they feel that they have a right to expect relief from many of these imposts, and a more careful scrutiny of the national budget seems to be in order. When one considers that after this war we shall have a national debt about five times the size of that of 1939 and a national budget not less than three times the highest pre-war figure, it is time we took the situation in hand. If the  ,
results desired seem difficult to achieve at this time owing to fixed charges, commitments, uncontrollable expenditures and the costs of social legislation, all of which are quite in order, then I say it is high time that steps be taken to cut down controllable expenditures, and cut them down to the bone where it is possible to do so.
I respectfully suggest that the country's business is very much like any other business, only on a much larger scale. Where the necessity exists in private business to reduce costs or else suffer extinction, remedies are not long in being found. Usually a situation such as this is carefully analysed and studied; expert advice is sought as to just wrhere the necessary remedies should and could be applied, and then they are applied.
As to government expenditures, I suggest that a special committee of the house be appointed to cooperate with the Minister of Finance in making an exhaustive study of governmental spending. Comparisons should be made between the ordinary expenses of carrying on the government in 1939 and in the present year. Recommendations could then be made as to what steps should be taken to straighten out the whole picture, so that taxes might be reduced and Canadian credit remain at a high level. I respectfully submit that unless early and energetic steps such as these are taken, the next victory loan may receive only lukewarm support in many sections of the country.
There is also little doubt that unless income taxpayers receive some measure of relief this year from their tax burdens, hardships will ensue and incentives to work and produce will be lost. Heavy war-time excess profits taxes on industry should also be removed if the government's own plans for jobs in the postwar period are to be successfully carried out. Psychologically, and from every other angle, the time is here for us to give serious consideration to these problems.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I at this first opportunity compliment you on the high honour that has been conferred upon you? I am sure that you will continue to exercise that necessary degree of tolerance and fairness expected from you, especially to the new members who are not so familiar with the rules, and who rise for the first time, I can assure you, with some trepidation.
May I also extend my congratulations to the mover (Mr. Benidickson) and the seconder (Mr. Langlois) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne? My most sincere congratulations go to these two hon. members,

The Address-Mr. Murphy
because they chose to serve their king and country in time of war. I am sure that no member of the government or of the other parties to our left will forget that sitting in the ranks of the Progressive Conservative party are also distinguished soldiers, including two holders of the Victoria Cross. To these hon. gentlemen I cannot find words to express my gratitude. It is indeed an honour to be associated with them. It is a healthy sign to see so many young members in this House of Commons, men who are entering the political arena for the first time.
I am very proud to represent the riding of Lambton West, which includes Sarnia, not only because it has the largest oil refinery in the British empire, not because it has also the Polymer Corporation, commonly known as the rubber plant, but because I hope to be of some service to my riding and my country. That is the reason why I am here. I maintain that one must accept his responsibility or take the consequences.
I was sorry, Mr. Speaker, as a new member to hear some of the members to your right and to your left charging the Progressive Conservative party with being responsible for stirring up disunity in the Dominion of Canada. I think that sort of debate is beneath the dignity of this house. Of one thing I am proud, namely, that members of our party cannot be charged, as can the members of some other parties in this house, with spread>-ing the gospel of class hatred, distrust and discontent. Of all hatreds within a country, class hatred is by far the most dangerous, and to those who for political purposes are playing around with such high explosives, may I suggest that before it is too late they desist from such contemptible tactics, and that instead of preaching blue ruin and hoping for a depression so that they can stir up more class hatred, they act as real Canadians and stop selling Canada short. I maintain that our party preached national unity from the Atlantic to the Pacific, and that all would have equal rights, with no favourtism to anyone. Apparently some parts of this great dominion did not choose to take the chance of being treated on an equal basis.
We were elected as members of our respective ridings, but if we are to discharge our responsibilities as members of this house we must have a national outlook and consider that each and everyone of us represents a united Canada. I can best picture my thought by a simple illustration of nine men-I use the figure nine purposely-with their arms so tied and bound that they could not feed
themselves and yet had plenty on the table in front of them. They solved their own problems by each feeding the one to his left.
I should like at this time to emphasize that it. is a distinct honour for me to represent Lambton West in this house. In 1943 I contested the riding of West Lambton in the provincial arena. The ridings of Lambton West and West Lambton differ somewhat in their boundaries, and in the 1943 provincial election the riding of West Lambton was won by the C.C.F. party by a small majority. That was, as hon. members all remember, the time when the Polymer Corporation was being rushed to completion, and some 4,000 temporary workers from other parts of Canada were engaged in that construction. I may say they did not repeat it on June 4 in the Ontario government election, but ran a low third, the Progressive Conservative of course winning.
Most hon. members know that the dominion riding of Lambton West has been traditionally Liberal. It had a Liberal representative ever since confederation except for one term, when it was ably represented by the highly respected and recently deceased Mr. Le Sueur. It is with great satisfaction I say that the C.C.F. candidate lost his deposit, and thereby helped our Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) to the tune of $200; and if they ever find another C.C.F. candidate we shall assure them of the same generosity. So, Mr. Speaker, I have reason to be proud of being the second representative of our party for Lambton West since confederation.
I should like to quojte from one of Canada's most popular and highly respected newspapers, the Windsor Star of last Friday:
As the Liberals and Progressive Conservatives are the only two parties with any claim to national status, they are the parties who have to look to seats in all parts of the dominion. The other parties do well in this province or that, but they are not national parties. They are sectional groups, speaking for one area only.
To all those who are on the right of you, Mr. Speaker, and to my left, I wish to say, listen to this, and this will be my eulogy of my leader:
John Bracken is doing all right as leader of the Progressive Conservatives. He is the type of man who wears well and gathers strength as he rolls along. He is never spectacular, but he is impressive.
I wish for a few moments to dwell on the more material angle of my riding. We have heard some reference to sugar beets and the scarcity of sugar. Sugar stocks at Wallace-burg, normally a high production area, are reported as nil and have resulted in the
The Address-Mr. Murphy

actual importation of 2,000,000 pounds of cane sugar. This action was necessary to provide consumers and processors with even their very much limited ration. We did grow great quantities of sugar beets in Lambton county; and knowing the reasons for the lessened production I did not relish the billboard advertising of some months ago by the wartime prices and trade board, to the effect that there was plenty of sugar in the sugar bowl.
There are two reasons why Lambton county produces less sugar beets than formerly. The first one is common to sugar beet producers >n. all parts of Canada; that is, the government's much-muddled man-power system or, should I say, lack of system. The second is a serious menace to the sugar beet industry in our locality. It is a fact not known to many hon. members, but I am assured it is known to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner). This disease is a nematode, affecting the sugar beet. The entomologists of the Department of Agriculture are well aware of this menace and have made some surveys concerning it. The disease is considered so injurious to the industry that farmers in certain areas are not permitted to ship their beets by truck to the factories but are compelled to ship by railroad. It is feared that in shipping by truck beets may fall off and spread the disease. This same nematode is what created such havoc among the sugar beet growers in Utah. The disease has already spread elsewhere in Ontario. It is a serious situation, and every effort must be made to control and eliminate it entirely; otherwise I fear for the sugar beet industry in Ontario.
Some months ago representation was made to the Minister of Agriculture to take further action, and at the same time representation was made to the minister of agriculture of Ontario. Two creeks, or rather small rivers, which drain thousands of acres of land in this area empty into lake Huron. I have known there to be as much as four and a half feet of sand washed into the mouths of these creeks or rivers, thus preventing proper drainage. As a result of this, vast areas are sometimes under water, which simply means that it accentuates the spread of the disease to other lands. Engineers have suggested that the only way to keep the mouths of these creeks open is by constructing breakwaters at the mouths. The mouths of these creeks are subject to dominion government regulation, and the dominion government is the only agent that can legally rectify the situation. The minister of agriculture of Ontario, realizing the seriousness of the situation, agreed to pay one third of the cost of these breakwaters
TMr. Murphy.]
if the dominion government and the drainage areas paid the balance. It is my earnest desire that the minister will again look into the matter and cooperate to, preserve the industry, since not only are all sugar beets subject to infection, but also table beets, carrots and other vegetables. The market gardeners are very much alarmed, and in my riding, owing to boat shipping facilities, market gardening is an industry of no mean proportions. We have many hundreds of acres in Lambton West used for no other purpose than raising vegetables.
At a later date I may have something further to contribute regarding the sugar beet industry, and I may not confine my remarks to the production of sugar beets.
The other subject which I wish to discuss for a few moments is the greatest potential industry in Canada-and I do not purpose to qualify that statement-that is, the tourist industry. Sarnia is within one day's automobile drive in the United States of America of as many people as are in the whole Dominion of Canada. It is little wonder, therefore, that I am and will continue to be interested in the tourist industry.
I have heard with interest of the scheme to beautify the nation's capital. I am in hearty accord with the idea of beautification, and suggest that at. Sarnia, where, as I said before, we are the front gate to so many millions of Americans, much could be done as a dominion government undertaking as part of the programme to promote and increase our tourist industry. Every port of entry into Canada gives the tourist his first picture and impression of our country, and I think the federal, government could and should lend its aid to the provincial and municipal authorities in the beautification of all these ports, through which flow these great streams of wealth, so essential to our national interests. We are fortunate in having courteous customs and immigration officials who faithfully accept their responsibilities and are a credit to the service. They are the first officials to greet these tourists. Might I at this juncture emphasize and endorse a plea for these competent men, that they receive a wage or remuneration commensurate with their duties and responsibilities. I am advised that they have not received the consideration to which they were and are entitled to monetarily. I believe I am right in saying that their scale of wages has not been raised except on a much too modest scale since 1925. Surely since the depression these men should receive decent wages. I maintain here and now that- a man qualified to enter

The Address-Mr. Murphy
the customs or immigration service should start at not less than $1,800 a year and not $1,200 or thereabouts, and that his increases should be on an equitable merit system.
For those hon. members who do not know, we have in Lambton West some ninety miles of shore line-partly along the St. Clair river and about sixty miles along the shores of lake Huron; a paradise for the American, and it is the American who is developing the shore line. Sarnia is less than sixty miles from Detroit. In 1939, 312,564 cars crossed the Blue Water bridge between Sarnia and Port Huron. Since that time, owing to the war and restrictions, the traffic has been less. But that will give the house an idea of what we may expect by considered planning.
It is not necessary that hon. members be told by me that we live in the best country in the world and that its changing beauty from east to west or north to south is unending and unequalled in its entirety. Nature has largely endowed our land with everything for the contentment and the happiness of our people and for those from other lands and climates who come to visit Canada. Canada must compete with the tourist attractions of other countries which are at all times being expanded and improved. One pre-war year alone, it is estimated, 16,000,000 United States tourists came to Canada, leaving in the country about $300 million. Ninety-five per cent of United States tourists came to Canada on "rubber tires".
We must be prepared not only for a return of this traffic in increased volume but also for those using the even more modern method of transportation, the aeroplane, which will open up our country to those even further removed from our boundaries than those to whom I have already referred.
The tourist traffic is valuable to our national life to a large extent and it might not be amiss to consider 1938 as a normal pre-war year. In 1938 Canada's credit balance of international payments amounted to $184,800,000. A favourable balance in the tourist trade amounted to $145,000,000, or 78-5 per cent of the total credit balance of international payments. If it had not been for the tourist trade. Canada's credit balance of international payments would have been negligible.
Much care and consideration is given by the government to the gold mining industry. Canada's credit balance in gold shipments amount to $156,500,000, or about nine per cent more than the tourist industry.
The Canadian government has established trade commissioners in many foreign countries to sell Canadian products. The credit balance
in the tourist trade as mentioned above amounted to $145 million as compared with $180,500,000 credit balance in the external trade, of all merchandise shipped from Canada, including agricultural products.
In 1938, Canada's tourist trade was of greater importance to Canada's national economy than any other single industry, with the exception of gold mining.
As a result of the Atlantic charter a great deal of consideration is being given to foreign trade. To offset this there will be a natural desire on the part of countries to be self-contained, particularly with regard to strategic materials.
Canada will continue to need foreign currency. As in the past one of the greatest sources of this currency will be tourist travel into Canada.
Canada has more at stake per capita in foreign trade than any other country in the world. Foreign travel in Canada, because of its advertising and educational value, could be used to create more foreign trade.
Advertising, better understanding, and a proper interpretation of Canada and Canadians, to foreign countries will be invaluable.
Canada is a large country populated by a relatively small number of people. There are several distinct population centres. Such conditions tend to create misunderstanding, resulting in local discontent and sectional prejudices. There is nothing which will counteract these unhappy conditions more effectively than travel.
The tourist traffic will compare more than favourably with any other industry in the amount of employment produced per dollar expended. Not only is there a direct benefit to farmers, retailers, purveyors of lodging and food, to travel systems, to gasoline and to other entrepreneurs, but this money creates much indirect employment because it passes through all channels of human enterprise. Even as the tourist traffic has become of primary importance to Switzerland, so the tourist traffic could be made of utmost value to Canada's national economy.
Canada abounds in natural attractions. From the Cabot trail in Cape Breton to lovely Victoria, every section has its own national appeal. Much can be done to exploit this.
Canada's facilities for recreation must be regarded as a natural resource to be developed under wise guidance for the benefit of the greatest possible number of people. They are a natural resource, just as our mines, forests, and farm lands are natural resources. They possess only one outstanding difference; they are not exhausted by use. Scenery,
The Address-Mr. Murphy

climate, and environment can be "sold" over and over again; can be drawn upon in perpetuity without any impairment of the original capital.
Development of Canada's recreational activities as a post-war enterprise has another important advantage over the production of material goods; there is practically no possibility, under reasonably prosperous conditions, of oversupplying the market. Aside from catering to the recreational needs of her own population, Canada has the advantage of lying alongside a great and populous country, perhaps the most travel-minded in the world, well disposed toward Canada and eager to make closer acquaintances. Development of Canada s recreational possibilities on a scale comparable with those of, say, Switzerland, would easily attain a monetary value in excess of a billion dollars a year.
For the past six years Canada has had a great corps of ambassadors all across the world, in the persons of those serving in His Majesty's uniform bearing Canada's name. These men and women have done much to advertise Canada abroad, although that was not their primary objective, but it should be the primary objective of the government of Canada to capitalize on their good work and foster the tourist trade to help make Canada a better country for these returned heroes to live in and as a lasting memorial to those who did not return.
Development of a recreational industry on a large scale will help to solve that problem by bringing a foreign market for our goods to Canada, instead of taking the goods to a foreign market over such obstacles as tariffs, exchange differentials and highly organized and well financed competition. Tourists are good spenders. They will consume substantial quantities of our agricultural products and will buy goods which have a Canadian flavour-maybe a Scotch flavour too-whether of handicraft or factory production, to take back home. They will furnish employment to large numbers of Canadians, who, in turn, because of their increased prosperity, will become greater consumers of Canadian products. They furnish increased revenues to transportation companies, hotels and all enterprises catering to the travelling public, to the wisespread advantage of Canadian economy.
Preservation and promotion of the health of the people must also occupy a prominent place in post-war planning. It would be a natural conclusion that residents of a great country like Canada, blessed with a healthful climate, descending from vigorous antecedents, with pioneer blood still in their veins, would rank high among all nations in the matter of 
general health. Any such pleasant conclusion has had a severe shock from the facts revealed by medical examination of recruits for war services. It appears, indeed, that Canada needs to take serious counsel with herself as to what she is going to do about the national health.
In a country like Canada, a land of great area and small population, and with even that small population clustered in distinct geographic groups, it is in the national interest that people should travel back and forth to become acquainted with each other, to see each other's problems and circumstances, to form friendships, to acquire the national rather than the parochial point of view.
What is true of the development of a real Oanadianism in Canada is equally true in the promotion of friendly foreign relationships. The good will toward Canada felt in the United States has undoubtedly been fostered by the great exchange of travel which in normal times occurs between these two countries. The extent to which that good will has prospered the cause of the united nations in the war would be hard to estimate. At present the interests of the two nations seem to be identical, but it may not always be so, and good will will be needed to assure cooperation and generous attitude on both sides toward issues which may arise in the future. What is true of relationships with the United States is also true, if in lesser degree, of relationships with the other American countries, and with the world as a whole. 'Making Canada the travel centre of the world after the war will pay dividends in international relationships, including opportunities for international trade, which probably could not be acquired by any other form of investment.
But people will travel. The money poured into the manufacture of munitions and supplies has transformed a large working-class population into a class of people with money to spend.
The tourist industry needs to be retooled and remodelled, to be put on as practical a hard rock basis as any manufacturing industry or service organization, for there is no real difference between them; in tourism we shall get customers only to the extent that our goods are better than those of our competitors.
Tourism to-day is no longer a parochial question. It extends beyond the confines of any one province, for each and every part of our vast dominion is beautiful and attractive. Each of the nine provinces that form our land has its own special attraction and charm for the visitor, and we should all work together, for the common good of the country, to bring about unity out of this very diversity.

The Address-Mr. Murphy
Speaking more specifically on the tourist industry and what it means to my riding, I said before that we had ninety miles of shore line. There are at least sixty miles of shore line between Sarnia and Grand Bend on lake Huron which to-day could be developed, as well as some thirty-five miles between Sarnia and Port Lambton along the St. Clair river. Some of it is now owned by Americans who have homes costing upwards of twenty-five thousand dollars. Right here let me emphasize that we welcome the United States tourist who comes even for a few hours; the one who comes for two weeks is worth more as is also the family who come for the season and it is they with whom my riding is chiefly concerned. We appreciate the travelling tourist and every effort should be made to have him return, and ultimately buy a piece of property and build a summer or semi-permanent home. In some parts of Canada, he is of greater value to us nationally. Let me now specify how important this type of tourist is to my riding in particular in that ninety miles of shore line, and the same can no doubt be said of other parts of Canada, but very few places in Canada are so fortunate in having so many so near. There is room for, say, in fifty miles, at least ten thousand homes, assuming it was highly developed and with fair-sized lots, and none of them more than four hundred feet from the shores of lake Huron or the banks of the river St. Clair. The property purchased would be in the neighbourhood of ten million dollars; the total building costs in the neighbourhood of fifty million dollars, and I have reason to believe that every American with a summer home spends on an average one thousand dollars annually. This in round figures is ten million dollars a year in our riding alone. The Americans will also buy many items of British manufacture in addition to Canadian-made goods. This extends our trade with Britain, and by these purchases we readily obtain foreign exchange including sterling so necessary in international trade. No other industry can compare with this. This is Canadian material used and made by Canadians and a means to-day to employ thousands of returning veterans, and in addition I say that the quicker we have the materials, the sooner we develop our greatest industry. We all agree that about eighty per cent of the cost of a frame house is labour, lumber and cement. At the moment we have a shortage of many building materials, including lumber.
May I submit that we need not have discovered ourselves in this position if the manpower of the nation had been properly used,

Between Sarnia and Grand Bend, a shore line of some sixty miles, there is not a harbour for the protection of commercial fishermen. Harbours are their only protection, and may I say in this connection that the two creeks or rivers I referred to previously as not having proper outlets, could be made into ideal natural harbours if proper and not necessarily expensive breakwaters were constructed. In closing, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say first, that I should like to learn the French language. I like your pleasant accent and, if I could, I would go down among your compatriots and teach them to sing, "I am beginning to see the light."
I earnestly hope that when the dominion-provincial conference again convenes the tourist industry will be a subject of major consideration, that the dominion and the provinces will correlate their activities so that we may take advantage of all that we have so much of an abundance to offer, and I can assure my hon. friends to the right of you, Mr. Speaker, that if the present government does the best it can possibly do, the Progressive Conservative government will finish the job after the next general election.
